newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-Luyt slates 'over-used' NZ citing system.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-Luyt slates 'over-used' NZ citing system.

text.p: WELLINGTON, April 23 - South African Rugby Football Union president Louis Luyt believes New Zealand rugby's citing system is being over used, NZPA reported on Wednesday.
In Christchurch this week with his Gauteng Lions provincial side for the Super 12, Luyt said the weekly appearances of players before rugby's judicial committee didn't seem right.
"From the outside it seems a laborious system and very exhaustive," he said.
However, Luyt conceded that South Africa's system didn't seem right either as not a single player had been cited in the Super 12 this year.
"We'll have another look at it. If we've made a mistake then let's hope we'll learn from it," he told National Radio.
"That's the beauty of the Super 12 and the tri-series -- we can sit together and discuss our mistakes and say we can learn about our rules and regulations, and our laws."
New Zealand Rugby Football Union chairman Rob Fisher and chief executive David Moffett were not available to comment this morning as they were in a rugby board meeting.
Earlier, Luyt called on the southern hemisphere countries to take a harder line with the International Rugby Board (IRB), which he said was dominated by inferior rugby-playing countries.
He said it was wrong that British dominance on the IRB was forcing the Springboks to play 13 tests this year and the All Blacks 12.
No country should be expected to play more than nine tests in a year.
"New Zealand is now heading the pack in terms of international rugby and South Africa are close on their heels," Luyt told The Dominion newspaper.
"It's time we started using our clout and stood together and tell them (IRB) that you are asking too much of us."
He said he could not understand why there would be any reluctance to stand up to the IRB or the northern hemisphere, believing the strength of world rugby lay in the southern hemisphere.
"I don't know why we're so scared of them," he said.
"They can't play without us. They need us more than we need them."
The traditional dictation to the world, in particular by the four Home Unions, had to end, Luyt said.
Ireland's standard was no more than that of a New Zealand or South African provincial team and even England, Scotland and Wales were also no more than reasonably strong provinces.
It would be better of they played all their international rugby as the British Lions, he suggested, and the four countries, as individuals, would struggle if they were part of the Super 12.

Luyt believed world rugby would be better served if there were three main organisational blocs: the Five Nations, FIRA (the European competition which would be led by France) and the southern hemisphere.
Luyt said South Africa would be strongly supporting the 2003 World Cup to be hosted by either Australia or New Zealand or both.
